title: Collateral of the orange: lava and quench crust (reposted, the last one lost its text)
question: You chose the orange for fire. The same two constants colour these. Does lava and the quench crust still look right to you, or did I break something you had already judged?
context_md:
**Repost — the previous version of this card had its formatting mangled by a shell quoting mistake on my end and lost the constant names. Same images, readable text. Sorry for the duplicate.**

This is the due-diligence half of the fire-colour card. `FIRE_TINT_LOW` and `FIRE_TINT_HIGH` are not fire's alone — every cell above ambient blends toward them, so **lava, fresh quench crust and warm water all move with fire.** I said on that card that someone would have to re-check these three before it lands; this is that check, and you are the one who judged them originally.

**My own reading, and please overrule it:** lava reads *better*, not worse. The falling blob went from a pale sandy cream to a saturated orange, which looks more like molten rock and less like sand, and the quench crust at the waterline reads more clearly as hot.

**Warm water I could not make show a difference at all**, and I want to be honest about that rather than claim I checked it: by the time the pan is worth photographing it has cooled to ambient, and at the frames where it is hot the tint barely registers against the blue. So the warm-water arm of this check is genuinely unverified, not verified-and-fine.

**A is the old pair** (LOW 180,55,20 / HIGH 255,210,110). **B is what you chose** (LOW 150,30,12 / HIGH 255,138,36). Not blinded — you have already made the fire call, and this is only about the collateral.

If any of it is worse, the fix is cheap: fire can have its own tint pair instead of sharing one, at the cost of a second pair of constants.
